course.title: From Polynomials to Étale Triple Covers
course.subtitle: A proof-based route to the announced three-dimensional Jacobian counterexample
course.description: A 66-week spiral course that begins with proof fundamentals and repeatedly revisits one factorization until the learner can reconstruct its algebraic, local, global, projective, and representation-theoretic meaning.

masteryDimensions.label: Proof reasoning
masteryDimensions.description: Logical structure, theorem use, and justified claims.

masteryDimensions.label: Procedural fluency
masteryDimensions.description: Reliable execution of calculations and standard methods.

masteryDimensions.label: Transfer
masteryDimensions.description: Choosing and adapting ideas in unfamiliar situations.

concepts.title: Functions and maps
concepts.summary: A function includes a domain, codomain, and assignment; a formula alone does not specify all three.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $f(z)=z^2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The expression $1/x$ without a stated domain is not yet a complete function.

concepts.title: Mathematical proof
concepts.summary: A proof makes assumptions, conclusions, and every inferential dependency explicit.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Showing both compositions are identities proves that two displayed maps are mutual inverses.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

concepts.title: Polynomial and binary form
concepts.summary: Polynomial arithmetic is the elementary surface of the entire construction.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous and hence is not a binary quadratic form.

concepts.title: Complex roots and multiplicity
concepts.summary: A cubic’s root multiplicities control both its discriminant and the fibers of the marked-root map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The multiplicity of $\zeta$ as a root of $p$ is the largest $m$ for which $(t-\zeta)^m$ divides $p(t)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(t-1)^2(t+2)$ has a double root at $1$ and a simple root at $-2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $p(\zeta)=0$ alone does not say that $\zeta$ is repeated.

concepts.title: Repeated-root criterion
concepts.summary: A root is repeated exactly when the polynomial and its derivative vanish there.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

concepts.title: Injectivity and bijectivity
concepts.summary: Injectivity is a global statement about the equality of images.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is injective.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is not globally injective.

concepts.title: Local versus global invertibility
concepts.summary: An invertible derivative yields a local inverse; it does not prove a globally one-to-one polynomial map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Local injectivity holds on a neighborhood of each point; global injectivity compares every pair of points in the full domain.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $w\mapsto w^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ has nonzero derivative everywhere but has three points in a generic fiber.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero Jacobian determinant is not, by itself, a proof of a polynomial inverse.

concepts.title: Vector spaces and dimension
concepts.summary: Binary forms of each degree form finite-dimensional complex vector spaces.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension $d+1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The set of degree-exactly-two polynomials is not closed under addition.

concepts.title: Symmetric powers
concepts.summary: Symmetric powers provide the natural representation spaces of binary forms.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$ is the quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$ identifying permutations of tensor factors.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^3(\mathbb C^2)$ is four-dimensional and models binary cubics.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The full tensor cube has dimension eight, not four.

concepts.title: Jacobian and total derivative
concepts.summary: The Jacobian matrix represents the derivative in coordinates.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

concepts.title: Inverse function theorem
concepts.summary: An invertible derivative gives a unique local inverse near the point.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $z\mapsto z^3$ has a local holomorphic inverse near every nonzero $z$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The theorem does not produce one inverse on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.

concepts.title: Group actions and symmetries
concepts.summary: Actions reveal the scaling direction multiplication forgets.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A group action of $G$ on $X$ assigns compatible transformations $g\cdot x$ for $g\in G$ and $x\in X$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ preserves $LQ$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An arbitrary coefficient change that does not respect composition is not a group action.

concepts.title: Ideals and quotient rings
concepts.summary: Equality on the variety is equality modulo its defining ideal.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

concepts.title: Localization
concepts.summary: Localization studies the open set where a chosen function is invertible.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X_a$ is studied by inverting $a$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An isomorphism after inverting $a$ does not describe the missing divisor $a=0$.

concepts.title: Projective roots
concepts.summary: Homogeneous coordinates keep the root at infinity visible.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: When $a=0$, the linear form $aT+bS$ has its root at $[1:0]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The affine expression $-b/a$ cannot describe the case $a=0$.

concepts.title: Resultant
concepts.summary: The resultant detects a shared projective root and restores the relative scaling direction lost by multiplication.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

concepts.title: Discriminant
concepts.summary: The discriminant vanishes exactly when a polynomial has a repeated root.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Disc}(C)$ is, up to normalization, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A cubic with three distinct roots has nonzero discriminant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero discriminant does not select one distinguished root.

concepts.title: Affine varieties
concepts.summary: Affine geometry translates polynomial equations into geometric objects.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X=\{\rho=1,\ ad+bc=1\}\subset\mathbb A^5$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A Euclidean neighborhood is generally not Zariski open.

concepts.title: Coordinate rings
concepts.summary: Regular functions on an affine variety form its coordinate ring.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X\cong\mathbb A^3$ follows from an explicit isomorphism of coordinate rings.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A rational expression with a denominator is not automatically a global regular function.

concepts.title: Tangent spaces and differentials
concepts.summary: The kernel of the multiplication differential is exactly the relative-scaling direction.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

concepts.title: Fibers and base change
concepts.summary: A fiber collects all points sharing one image; base change restricts a map while preserving étaleness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

concepts.title: Étale maps
concepts.summary: Étaleness is the algebraic form of local biholomorphic behavior and is stable under base change.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

concepts.title: Properness and nonproperness
concepts.summary: Nonproperness allows sheets of a local inverse to escape through the boundary.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

concepts.title: The projective line
concepts.summary: $\mathbb P^1$ completes the affine root chart by adding the point at infinity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

concepts.title: Marked-root incidence
concepts.summary: The global map forgets which simple projective root was chosen.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

concepts.title: Covering maps
concepts.summary: Covering-space language distinguishes local sheet structure from global properness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A covering map evenly covers a neighborhood of every base point by disjoint homeomorphic sheets.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $z\mapsto z^n$ is an $n$-sheeted covering of $\mathbb C^\times$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A local homeomorphism with escaping sheets need not be a covering map.

concepts.title: $SL_2$ and binary forms
concepts.summary: $SL_2$ acts by change of variables on binary forms and makes multiplication equivariant.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $SL_2$ acts on $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ through its action on the variables $S,T$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Polynomial multiplication is $SL_2$-equivariant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A coordinate formula that changes under basis change without an equivariance law is not intrinsic.

concepts.title: Torus weights and gradings
concepts.summary: The residual scaling action predicts the useful affine coordinates and their degrees.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\deg a=1$, $\deg y=-1$, and $\deg z=-2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Ordinary polynomial degree and torus weight are different gradings.

concepts.title: Normal jets
concepts.summary: Corrected first and second normal coefficients motivate the coordinates $y$ and $z$ along $a=0$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

concepts.title: The normalized factorization threefold
concepts.summary: The central space $X$ normalizes both the resultant and one cubic coefficient and is polynomially isomorphic to affine three-space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

concepts.title: The Keller map
concepts.summary: Composing the affine coordinates with the cubic coefficient map yields the explicit constant-Jacobian polynomial map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

modules.title: Term 0 · Algebra and proof bridge
modules.description: Make algebraic manipulation reliable while changing from calculating answers to justifying every claim.

modules.title: Term 1 · Linear algebra, derivatives, and local inversion
modules.description: Understand Jacobians as derivatives of maps between vector spaces rather than determinant recipes.

modules.title: Term 2 · Abstract algebra, resultants, and discriminants
modules.description: Develop the algebra of factorization spaces and resultant normalization.

modules.title: Term 3 · Commutative algebra and affine algebraic geometry
modules.description: Change viewpoint from equations in complex affine space to varieties, coordinate rings, and étale maps.

modules.title: Term 4 · Projective geometry, incidence, and covering spaces
modules.description: Explain the global three-to-one geometry through marked projective roots and escaping sheets.

modules.title: Term 5 · $SL_2$, torus weights, and the affine-space miracle
modules.description: Motivate the affine coordinates through symmetry, weights, and normal jets.

modules.title: Term 6 · Research seminar
modules.description: Reconstruct, classify, verify, and present the full counterexample construction.

content.title: Week 1 in the spiral

## Study focus

Functions, domains, codomains, composition, inverses, graph versus formula, linear and quadratic equations, exponent rules, and rational expressions.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Functions and maps

A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.

**Example.** $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $f(z)=z^2$.

**Nonexample.** The expression $1/x$ without a stated domain is not yet a complete function.

### Injectivity and bijectivity

$f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.

**Example.** $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is injective.

**Nonexample.** $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is not globally injective.

content.title: Pass condition
content.markdown: You can manipulate a rational polynomial expression reliably and state the difference between a function, its formula, its graph, and its image.

## Study focus

Polynomial addition, multiplication, long division, factor theorem, remainder theorem, multiplicity of a root, and degree.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Polynomial and binary form

A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.

**Example.** $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic.

**Nonexample.** $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous and hence is not a binary quadratic form.

### Mathematical proof

A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

**Example.** Showing both compositions are identities proves that two displayed maps are mutual inverses.

**Nonexample.** Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

content.title: Week 3 in the spiral
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of complex numbers and roots.

## Study focus

Complex arithmetic, modulus and argument, polar form, roots of unity, the fundamental theorem of algebra as a usable theorem, and repeated roots.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Complex roots and multiplicity

The multiplicity of $\zeta$ as a root of $p$ is the largest $m$ for which $(t-\zeta)^m$ divides $p(t)$.

**Example.** $(t-1)^2(t+2)$ has a double root at $1$ and a simple root at $-2$.

**Nonexample.** $p(\zeta)=0$ alone does not say that $\zeta$ is repeated.

### Repeated-root criterion

$\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

**Example.** For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

**Nonexample.** For $p(t)=t-1$, $p(1)=0$ but $p'(1)=1$.

content.title: Pass condition
content.markdown: You can explain why a cubic generically has three choices of distinguished root.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $p(t)=(t-\zeta)^m q(t)$ with $m\ge2$, differentiation shows both terms in $p'$ contain a factor $t-\zeta$, so $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$. Conversely, $p(\zeta)=0$ gives $p=(t-\zeta)q$. Differentiating gives $p'=q+(t-\zeta)q'$, hence $p'(\zeta)=q(\zeta)$. If this is zero, the factor theorem gives $q=(t-\zeta)r$, so $(t-\zeta)^2$ divides $p$.

content.title: Week 4 in the spiral
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of sets and notation.

## Study focus

BOP Chapter 1: sets, subsets, Cartesian products, union, intersection, complements, indexed families, and set-builder notation.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Functions and maps

A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.

**Example.** $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $f(z)=z^2$.

**Nonexample.** The expression $1/x$ without a stated domain is not yet a complete function.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Mathematical proof

A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

**Example.** Showing both compositions are identities proves that two displayed maps are mutual inverses.

**Nonexample.** Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

### Injectivity and bijectivity

$f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.

**Example.** $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is injective.

**Nonexample.** $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is not globally injective.

## Concept grounding

### Mathematical proof

A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

**Example.** Showing both compositions are identities proves that two displayed maps are mutual inverses.

**Nonexample.** Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

### Repeated-root criterion

$\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

**Example.** For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

**Nonexample.** For $p(t)=t-1$, $p(1)=0$ but $p'(1)=1$.

content.title: Day 1 method

## Concept grounding

### Functions and maps

A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.

**Example.** $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $f(z)=z^2$.

**Nonexample.** The expression $1/x$ without a stated domain is not yet a complete function.

### Injectivity and bijectivity

$f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.

**Example.** $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is injective.

**Nonexample.** $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is not globally injective.

### Mathematical proof

A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

**Example.** Showing both compositions are identities proves that two displayed maps are mutual inverses.

**Nonexample.** Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

Prove $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)=d+1$.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Vector spaces and dimension:** A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.
- **Symmetric powers:** $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$ is the quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$ identifying permutations of tensor factors.

## Authored checks

1. Prove that the space of degree-$\leq d$ polynomials has dimension (d+1).
2. Show: $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)=d+1.$
3. Write explicit bases for binary linear, quadratic, and cubic forms.
4. Prove that every two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have equal size.

## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

---

Week 9: ## Required conclusion

Move between equations, matrices, kernels, images, and affine solution sets.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Vector spaces and dimension:** A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.

## Authored checks

1. Solve systems by elimination.
2. Interpret a solution set as an affine subspace.
3. Compute kernels and images of simple matrix maps.
4. Relate the number of free variables to dimension.

## Passing standard

You can move between equations, matrices, and geometric solution sets.

---

Week 7: ## Required conclusion

Disprove false universal statements and locate an invalid division by zero.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Mathematical proof:** A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.
- **Repeated-root criterion:** $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

## Authored checks

1. Disprove five plausible but false polynomial statements.
2. Use induction to derive the binomial theorem.
3. Prove an equivalence by establishing both implications.
4. Find exactly where an invalid proof silently divides by zero.

## Passing standard

You habitually test universal statements against small examples and exceptional cases such as $a=0$.

---

Week 2: ## Required conclusion

Expand $(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)$ and justify each coefficient.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Polynomial and binary form:** A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.
- **Mathematical proof:** A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

## Authored checks

1. Prove that if $p(\alpha)=0$, then $t-\alpha$ divides $p(t)$.
2. Prove that a nonzero polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots.
3. Expand $(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)$ and identify all four coefficients.
4. Derive Viète's formulas for a monic quadratic and cubic.

## Passing standard

You can pass freely between a cubic's expanded form and a chosen linear-times-quadratic factorization.

Linear maps, change of basis, matrix representations, compositions, and inverses.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Vector spaces and dimension

A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension $d+1$.

**Nonexample.** The set of degree-exactly-two polynomials is not closed under addition.

### Polynomial and binary form

A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.

**Example.** $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic.

**Nonexample.** $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous and hence is not a binary quadratic form.

Week 8: ## Required conclusion

Prove that two displayed polynomial maps are mutual inverses by checking both compositions.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Functions and maps:** A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.

1. ## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

---

Week 3: ## Required conclusion

Prove the repeated-root criterion and classify cubic multiplicities.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Complex roots and multiplicity:** The multiplicity of $\zeta$ as a root of $p$ is the largest $m$ for which $(t-\zeta)^m$ divides $p(t)$.
- **Repeated-root criterion:** $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

1. Find all $n$-th roots of unity.
2. Draw the roots of several cubics in the complex plane.
3. Prove: $\alpha\text{ is a repeated root of }p \iff p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0.$
4. Classify cubics by root multiplicity: $1+1+1,\qquad 2+1,\qquad 3.$

## Passing standard

You can explain why a cubic generically has three choices of distinguished root.

For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

**Example.** For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Nonexample.** A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

### Vector spaces and dimension

A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension $d+1$.

**Nonexample.** The set of degree-exactly-two polynomials is not closed under addition.

## Study focus

Total derivative, partial derivatives, directional derivatives, Jacobian matrices, and the chain rule.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Jacobian and total derivative

For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

**Example.** For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Nonexample.** A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Nonexample.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

content.title: Week 17 in the spiral
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of inverse and implicit function theorems.

## Study focus

Precise hypotheses and conclusions of the inverse and implicit function theorems.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Inverse function theorem

If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.

**Example.** $z\mapsto z^3$ has a local holomorphic inverse near every nonzero $z$.

**Nonexample.** The theorem does not produce one inverse on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.

### Local versus global invertibility

Local injectivity holds on a neighborhood of each point; global injectivity compares every pair of points in the full domain.

**Example.** $w\mapsto w^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ has nonzero derivative everywhere but has three points in a generic fiber.

**Nonexample.** A nonzero Jacobian determinant is not, by itself, a proof of a polynomial inverse.

### Jacobian and total derivative

For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

**Example.** For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Nonexample.** A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

content.markdown: You can state the inverse function theorem without accidentally claiming global invertibility.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Inverse function theorem

If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.

**Example.** $z\mapsto z^3$ has a local holomorphic inverse near every nonzero $z$.

**Nonexample.** The theorem does not produce one inverse on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.

### Repeated-root criterion

$\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

**Example.** For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

**Nonexample.** For $p(t)=t-1$, $p(1)=0$ but $p'(1)=1$.

### Local versus global invertibility

Local injectivity holds on a neighborhood of each point; global injectivity compares every pair of points in the full domain.

**Example.** $w\mapsto w^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ has nonzero derivative everywhere but has three points in a generic fiber.

**Nonexample.** A nonzero Jacobian determinant is not, by itself, a proof of a polynomial inverse.

- **Inverse function theorem:** If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.
- **Repeated-root criterion:** $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Jacobian and total derivative:** For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

- **Polynomial and binary form:** A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.

Week 3: ## Required conclusion

Prove the repeated-root criterion and classify cubic multiplicities.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Complex roots and multiplicity:** The multiplicity of $\zeta$ as a root of $p$ is the largest $m$ for which $(t-\zeta)^m$ divides $p(t)$.

Distinguish an orbit space from a normalized slice.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Group actions and symmetries:** A group action of $G$ on $X$ assigns compatible transformations $g\cdot x$ for $g\in G$ and $x\in X$.
- **Torus weights and gradings:** A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.

Week 18: ## Required conclusion

Explain why simple roots vary locally while repeated roots do not define unique local branches.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Inverse function theorem:** If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.
- **Repeated-root criterion:** $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.
- **Local versus global invertibility:** Local injectivity holds on a neighborhood of each point; global injectivity compares every pair of points in the full domain.

## Authored checks

1. Show that a simple root varies holomorphically under small coefficient perturbations.
2. Show why a repeated root does not define a unique local root branch.
3. Distinguish local biholomorphism, covering map, proper map, and global bijection.
4. Write a two-page explanation of why constant Jacobian does not visibly imply global injectivity.

## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

---

Week 13: ## Required conclusion

Derive determinant properties from multilinearity and interpret invertibility geometrically.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Jacobian and total derivative:** For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.
- **Vector spaces and dimension:** A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.

## Authored checks

1. Derive determinant properties from multilinearity.
2. Prove $\det(AB)=\det A\det B.$
3. Compute block-triangular determinants.
4. Derive the $2\times2$ Schur-complement formula in the invertible-block case.

## Passing standard

A determinant is no longer merely an expansion by minors.

---

Translate local injectivity and the Jacobian conjecture into precise quantified language.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Mathematical proof:** A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.
- **Injectivity and bijectivity:** $f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Nonexample.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

### Torus weights and gradings

A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.

**Example.** $\deg a=1$, $\deg y=-1$, and $\deg z=-2$.

**Nonexample.** Ordinary polynomial degree and torus weight are different gradings.

## Study focus

Localization $A_f$, inverting one element, distinguished open sets, and Laurent polynomials.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Localization

$A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.

**Example.** $X_a$ is studied by inverting $a$.

**Nonexample.** An isomorphism after inverting $a$ does not describe the missing divisor $a=0$.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Nonexample.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of homogeneous polynomials and projective roots.

## Study focus

Binary forms, homogeneous coordinates, affine charts of $\mathbb P^1$, and roots at infinity.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Projective roots

A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.

**Example.** When $a=0$, the linear form $aT+bS$ has its root at $[1:0]$.

**Nonexample.** The affine expression $-b/a$ cannot describe the case $a=0$.

### The projective line

$\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.

**Example.** The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.

**Nonexample.** $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Resultant

$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Nonexample.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

### Projective roots

A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.

## Study focus

Discriminant as a symmetric function of root differences and as a resultant: $\operatorname{Disc}(C) \sim\operatorname{Res}(C,C').$

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Discriminant

$\operatorname{Disc}(C)$ is, up to normalization, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$.

**Example.** A cubic with three distinct roots has nonzero discriminant.

**Nonexample.** A nonzero discriminant does not select one distinguished root.

### Repeated-root criterion

$\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.

**Example.** For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

**Nonexample.** For $p(t)=t-1$, $p(1)=0$ but $p'(1)=1$.

content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Group actions and symmetries

A group action of $G$ on $X$ assigns compatible transformations $g\cdot x$ for $g\in G$ and $x\in X$.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ preserves $LQ$.

**Nonexample.** An arbitrary coefficient change that does not respect composition is not a group action.

### Resultant

$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Nonexample.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Nonexample.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

Prove that the cubic discriminant vanishes exactly for a repeated root.

- **Discriminant:** $\operatorname{Disc}(C)$ is, up to normalization, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$.

Week 26: ## Required conclusion

Explain the projective root of $aT+bS$ when $a=0$.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Projective roots:** A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.

- **Ideals and quotient rings:** $A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.
- **Polynomial and binary form:** A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.

## Authored checks

2. Compare polynomial and rational functions.

Derive determinant properties from multilinearity and interpret invertibility geometrically.

content.title: Day 1 method

## Concept grounding

### Affine varieties

An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.

**Example.** $X=\{\rho=1,\ ad+bc=1\}\subset\mathbb A^5$.

**Nonexample.** A Euclidean neighborhood is generally not Zariski open.

### Polynomial and binary form

A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.

**Example.** $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic.

**Nonexample.** $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous and hence is not a binary quadratic form.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Nonexample.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

### Jacobian and total derivative

For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

**Example.** For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Nonexample.** A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

### Affine varieties

An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.

**Example.** $X=\{\rho=1,\ ad+bc=1\}\subset\mathbb A^5$.

**Nonexample.** A Euclidean neighborhood is generally not Zariski open.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Nonexample.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

content.title: Day 1 method

## Concept grounding

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Nonexample.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

## Study focus

Kähler differentials at an example-driven level, unramifiedness, flatness, and étaleness. Use two parallel definitions:
- analytically: a local biholomorphism
- algebraically: a finite-presentation map that is flat and unramified.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Nonexample.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Nonexample.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

### Inverse function theorem

If $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism or biholomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.

**Example.** $z\mapsto z^3$ has a local holomorphic inverse near every nonzero $z$.

**Nonexample.** The theorem does not produce one inverse on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.

## Concept grounding

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Nonexample.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

### Coordinate rings

$\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.

**Example.** $X\cong\mathbb A^3$ follows from an explicit isomorphism of coordinate rings.

**Nonexample.** A rational expression with a denominator is not automatically a global regular function.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Nonexample.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Nonexample.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

### Resultant

$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Nonexample.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Nonexample.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Coprimality follows from nonzero resultant. If $\dot LQ+L\dot Q=0$, divisibility gives $\dot L=\lambda L$ and $\dot Q=-\lambda Q$, so the multiplication differential has the one-dimensional relative-scaling kernel. Along this vector the resultant’s bidegree $(2,1)$ gives derivative $\lambda\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$, which is nonzero unless $\lambda=0$. Hence $d\Phi$ is injective; source and target both have dimension five, so it is an isomorphism.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of the projective line.

## Study focus

$\mathbb P^1$, homogeneous coordinates, affine charts, projective roots, and the action of $PGL_2$.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### The projective line

$\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.

**Example.** The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.

**Nonexample.** $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

### Projective roots

A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.

**Example.** When $a=0$, the linear form $aT+bS$ has its root at $[1:0]$.

**Nonexample.** The affine expression $-b/a$ cannot describe the case $a=0$.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of symmetric powers of $\mathbb p^1$.

## Study focus

$\operatorname{Sym}^n(\mathbb P^1) \cong \mathbb P^n.$ Understand this concretely through coefficients of binary forms, not initially through abstract quotient constructions.

content.title: Day 1 method

### Symmetric powers

$\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$ is the quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$ identifying permutations of tensor factors.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Sym}^3(\mathbb C^2)$ is four-dimensional and models binary cubics.

**Nonexample.** The full tensor cube has dimension eight, not four.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Nonexample.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### The projective line

$\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.

**Example.** The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.

**Nonexample.** $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

## Concept grounding

### The projective line

$\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.

**Example.** The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.

**Nonexample.** $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

$\operatorname{Disc}(C)$ is, up to normalization, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$.

**Example.** A cubic with three distinct roots has nonzero discriminant.

**Nonexample.** A nonzero discriminant does not select one distinguished root.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Covering maps

A covering map evenly covers a neighborhood of every base point by disjoint homeomorphic sheets.

**Example.** $z\mapsto z^n$ is an $n$-sheeted covering of $\mathbb C^\times$.

**Nonexample.** A local homeomorphism with escaping sheets need not be a covering map.

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Nonexample.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

content.title: Day 1 method

## Concept grounding

**Nonexample.** A nonzero Jacobian determinant is not, by itself, a proof of a polynomial inverse.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Nonexample.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

### Covering maps

A covering map evenly covers a neighborhood of every base point by disjoint homeomorphic sheets.

**Example.** $z\mapsto z^n$ is an $n$-sheeted covering of $\mathbb C^\times$.

**Nonexample.** A local homeomorphism with escaping sheets need not be a covering map.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Nonexample.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### Resultant

$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Example.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Nonexample.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Nonexample.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Nonexample.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

## Concept grounding

### Group actions and symmetries

A group action of $G$ on $X$ assigns compatible transformations $g\cdot x$ for $g\in G$ and $x\in X$.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ preserves $LQ$.

**Nonexample.** An arbitrary coefficient change that does not respect composition is not a group action.

### $SL_2$ and binary forms

$SL_2$ acts on $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ through its action on the variables $S,T$.

**Example.** Polynomial multiplication is $SL_2$-equivariant.

**Nonexample.** A coordinate formula that changes under basis change without an equivariance law is not intrinsic.

## Concept grounding

A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.

**Nonexample.** An arbitrary coefficient change that does not respect composition is not a group action.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Nonexample.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Nonexample.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

Week 48: ## Required conclusion

Prove $z\mapsto z^n$ is locally injective and globally $n$-to-one on $\mathbb C^\times$.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Covering maps:** A covering map evenly covers a neighborhood of every base point by disjoint homeomorphic sheets.

3. Consequently $d\Phi$ is an isomorphism.
4. Therefore $\Phi$ is étale on the nonzero-resultant locus.

content.title: Day 1 method

## Concept grounding

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Nonexample.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Nonexample.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

**Example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

## Concept grounding

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Nonexample.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Nonexample.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Nonexample.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Nonexample.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Nonexample.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

## Required conclusion

Compute a three-point fiber and distinguish degree, cardinality, ramification, and nonproperness.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Fibers and base change:** The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.
- **Marked-root incidence:** A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.
- **Properness and nonproperness:** Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

## Authored checks

1. identify the three simple roots;
2. normalize each corresponding factorization to resultant $1$;
3. derive the three preimages;
4. compute one explicit fiber containing three points. Then analyze:
- a cubic with one double and one simple root
- a triple-root cubic
- how the admissible marked roots change. Clearly distinguish:
- generic degree
- actual fiber cardinality
- ramification
- nonproperness
- omitted points. Some of the more detailed descriptions of the asymptotic set discussed earlier should be independently rechecked rather than accepted automatically.

## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

content.title: Day 1 method
content.markdown: Read the definitions actively: rewrite them and test the boundary cases.

## Concept grounding

### The Keller map

$G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

**Example.** $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.

**Nonexample.** A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Nonexample.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Nonexample.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Nonexample.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

- **Normal jets:** $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

## Authored checks

1. Prove the polynomial isomorphism $\mathbb A^3_{a,y,z}\longrightarrow X$ using $\begin{aligned} b&=1+ay,\ c&=1-\frac32ay+a^2z,\ d&=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz,\ e&=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z. \end{aligned}$ Prove the inverse: $y=2bd-ae,$ $z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e.$ Your written solution must establish both compositions exactly.

## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.

---

Week 50: ## Required conclusion

Write the normalized marked-root account of local invertibility and generic degree three.

## Definitions and facts the proof may use

- **Marked-root incidence:** A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.
- **Resultant:** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.
- **Properness and nonproperness:** Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.
- **Étale maps:** For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

## Authored checks

1. a point of $X$ as a normalized factorization $C=LQ$;
2. a generic cubic having three preimages;
3. resultant $1$ selecting a unique scaling;
4. the map being locally invertible because the marked root is simple;
5. noninjectivity coming from the three possible marked roots;
6. failure of finiteness coming from the boundary at infinity.

## Passing standard

The conclusion must follow from stated hypotheses with every exceptional case addressed.
